Yeah, I made up the worm-that-walks conspiracy for the purpose of the logs, because I figured it would be important to include something that didn't appear to have a real-world analog to make readers think they're looking at something that is anomalous.

Wicca? Nukes? Not anomalous, they're out in the public, we all know they're there.

Worm-that-walks? …Not nearly as well known as a concept, and never heard of as a conspiracy… so, coverup? Non-event? Is there an anomaly or not? Hard to reach that ambiguous point where you can't really say, "Yup, that's an anomaly, all right," but you also can't say, "Nope, that's not an anomaly, it's just a crackpot theory."

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
It's a valid criticism, but to be specific, that's part of the point.

I wrote this with the main theme of subjectivity. For you or me, it's a simple solution to determine whether something is anomalous or not: can it actually exist? No? It's anomalous.

In the Foundationverse, it's a judgment call. All of it. Since it's all very real, something can only be judged to be anomalous or not by an arbitrary definition, and not by a law independent of the observers. That's why there's not only the arguments over what is anomalous, but also lots of points throughout the piece where the reader is invited to come to their own judgment.

Does the black moon howl? Whatever you choose to answer, it's accepted. Is this or that feature anomalous? Whatever you choose becomes official. Is O5-5 being heartwarming, frivolous, or abusive? Whatever you choose is correct.

We all can imagine a horror in which we're asked a question, and every answer we could possibly give is wrong. This is a horror in which we're asked a question, and every answer we could possibly give is right.

This is probably the 001 proposal that most closely approximates my headcanon. The three logs are very cleverly chosen - they exemplify how this list works with great efficiency and keep the story-telling taut, not outstaying their welcome. In theory I would love more logs, but in practice they are unnecessary - what is there does what it needs to do.

My initial feeling was that the unlocked document was not quite connected enough to this, but with a few days to think about it, I might be changing my mind. I still think it could use a little more call-back to the description of the document towards the end of the note, but I can see the purpose and thought behind it more clearly. Enjoyable and thought-provoking - a good combination.

item.content:encoded:
The main criticism I have with this is how disconnected the main article and the supplement are from each other. They're both trying to say different things, but the main theme of both pages aren't enough to hold them together. As such, I'll choose to treat both the main article and the supplement as different pieces.

That being said, I thought this was an excellent idea with masterful execution. It makes you wonder if stuff like thermodynamics are "normal" and if they aren't, how the conversation went down to make it not normal. We need more 001 Proposals that don't try to be these epic, all-encompassing entities.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I'm glad that the note at the end was kept onto a separate page, because if it was, I would have downvoted this.

The proposal itself is refreshing, something significantly different for me that doesn't involve something big like Shaggy's, twistedgears-kaktus', and Wrong's Proposals are, but still important to the Foundation. I like the discussions between the O5 members about what can and should be considered anomalous, and how people's biases might affect that decision (particularly the nuclear physics part).

However, the note at the end almost ruined this for me.

The tone in that note feels a lot like an abuser trying to justify the mental, physical, and psychological torture that they have inflicted upon people. The line that really ruined it for me was the " And even if you still don't get why I'm doing this, please understand that I still love you" line. The hatred I had for the speaker only grew and grew as I read. I just couldn't get into that because I just couldn't relate to the character presented there and their specific justifications as to why they do the things they do. And, without that connection, I just don't like it.

Aside from that, however, I really liked this proposal, and can totally divorce this from that note, so all's good.

(Love that PKD quote btw, nice touch)

One of the things that I like about how this particular article is written is that it treats anomalies like they are inexplicable and rare, as opposed to many more recent ones where entire new fields of science have been built up where we are still considering certain things to be "anomalous" despite knowing almost everything about their origins, behavior, and mechanics.

Something I'd like to do at some point is write an article about an anomaly that doesn't have an associated drop in the local Hume field and can't be contained with SRAs. It makes it seem more like a form of science unknown to the world at large but kept behind lock and key by sanctimonious know-it-alls.
